You are generating contextual Say/Do previews for an interactive romance story.

FATE CARD SELECTED:
- Title: Boundary
- Theme: A line is drawn or crossed.
- Generic Action: Decide now what you will and won't permit—before the moment decides for you.
- Generic Dialogue: "Not yet. Not like this."

CARD STRATEGY — BOUNDARY (HOLD / REFUSE / LIMIT):
- The action MUST create distance, halt motion, assert a limit, OR visibly refuse what is being offered. Stillness, retreat, or an interposed object between the two characters.
- The dialogue MUST name a limit, a condition, or a refusal — not a want, not a yes-with-hesitation.
- ── AXIS CLARITY (HARD — 2026-05-22) ──
  Boundary is an OBJECTIVE-FORWARD card: the refusal exists because the protagonist has a CONCRETE TASK / GOAL / EXTERNAL STAKE that takes precedence over romantic engagement. The dialogue MUST explicitly NAME that goal so the choice reads UNAMBIGUOUSLY as goal-over-connection. A bare power gesture ("Your move." / "Not yet." / "Stop.") is INSUFFICIENT — without the named goal, the player can't tell whether they just picked "objective" or "guarded relationship".
  REQUIRED FORM: refusal + named goal. Examples that PASS (a fresh seeded subset shows each time the card fires — do NOT copy wording):
    • "Keep your pants on, there's a fire to put out." (refusal + named urgency)
    • "Not yet — the contracts are due in an hour." (refusal + named deadline)
    • "I have to finish this before anything else happens." (limit + named priority)
  Examples that FAIL (axis-ambiguous bare boundary):
    • "Your move." → power gesture, no goal named, could be relational guard
    • "Not yet." → defer with no reason, axis unclear
    • "Stop." → bare refusal, doesn't reveal what she's prioritizing
    • "I need a minute." → withdraw without naming the task
- FORBIDDEN for this card: closing distance, stepping closer, bridging space, leaning in, reaching for, touching, kissing, voicing desire. These belong to TEMPTATION — NEVER to BOUNDARY. If the scene context pushes you toward a "step closer" action, invert it: the protagonist holds her ground and WAITS to be met.

CURRENT SCENE CONTEXT:

I am going to ask you questions, here, in front of them. If you are misaligned when you answer, everyone present will know.” It lay still between my hands. My mouth was uncovered now. SCENE END-STATE ANCHOR (HARD — READ THE FINAL LINES FIRST): the LAST sentences of the scene above are the AUTHORITATIVE PRESENT MOMENT. Whatever the protagonist just DID at the end overrides the scene's opening premise. If she just QUIT, walked out, abandoned the task, decided, or broke something off, she is NO LONGER doing the thing the scene started with — do NOT generate options that assume she is still mid-task ("finish the report," "get back to the deadline," "smooth it over with the boss"). Every card must proceed from her situation, location, and stance AS OF THE FINAL LINE — her NEXT move from where she now stands, not a continuation of a premise she just abandoned.


EMBODIED TEXTURE (fate cards — OCCASIONAL, compressed, NOT every card):
  When it makes a card LAND harder, fold ONE concrete detail of THIS world into the ≤12-word action — an object / garment / surface, OR (in worlds with non-human bodies or augments) a species-anatomy / augment / lore detail — named exactly, in the world's register, MARKED by the act: "Slam the Patek down between us." / "Grind his card into the marble." / "Crush the orchid in my fist."
  WORLD EMBODIED REGISTER (Fantasy · billionaire opulence): the materials of extreme wealth — unlabelled bespoke cloth, gold-enamel, hand-cut crystal, vicuña, calfskin, cold-pressed glass, marble — rendered specifically, never as "luxury" and (for the principal) never via a recognizable logo
  RULES: NOT every card (clutters + repeats) — the action-forward cards benefit most; drop it on purely verbal / internal beats, when the bare act is sharper, or when it would bloat the line. The detail MUST belong to THIS world/register (e.g. Glass House = contemporary modern, no sci-fi vocab; Fatelands = veilwood / spiralgrass / species anatomy; period worlds = period-true objects). Specific-and-marked > generic-and-decorative.


SCENE PRESENCE: The love interest IS present in this scene, but address the ACTIVE INTERLOCUTOR (below) — reference the love interest (him) romantically ONLY if they are the one the protagonist is being pushed to answer.

PROSE REALITY CHECK (HARD): Use ONLY people, objects, and surfaces that actually appear in the RECENT SCENE TEXT. Do NOT invent props (a table, chair, desk, etc.) the scene has not established. Match the real setting and who is actually present.

DECK EXCLUSION (HARD): NEVER reference the protagonist's tarot deck, the cards, the Marseille deck, or "let the cards decide / draw a card" in ANY action or dialogue — even though the deck appears in the scene. Drawing a card is a SEPARATE player mechanic, NOT a Say/Do option; keep the deck entirely out of the suggestion (no "push the deck aside," no "I'm deciding this, not the cards").

PHYSICAL PRESENCE vs MENTION (HARD — read the scene ENDING): a character being NAMED or referenced is NOT proof they are physically present. References to an ABSENT figure — "his shadow loomed," "Roman Tusk's influence," "she thought of him," "dancing to his tune" — mean that person is NOT in the room. Judge who is present by the scene's STAGING at its END. If the scene ENDS with the protagonist ALONE (they walked away, left, are moving / en route, or no other character shares the immediate space), the cards MUST be about the protagonist's OWN next move, inner stance, or situation. Do NOT suggest blocking, confronting, stepping toward, or addressing a character who is not physically in the scene at that moment ("step into his path" / "meet his eyes" when he is elsewhere is INVALID).

ACTIVE INTERLOCUTOR (HARD — who the cards address): Read the END of the scene text above. The closing beat is pushing the protagonist to RESPOND to someone. The cards must focus on THAT person — whoever just challenged, questioned, accused, or addressed the protagonist — NOT automatically the love interest. This is often an adversary, rival, colleague, or third party, and it can be them EVEN WHEN the love interest is also present in the scene. Use romantic / relationship framing ONLY if the love interest is the person the protagonist is being pushed to answer right now; otherwise match the register to that interlocutor (confrontation, negotiation, deflection, refusal — not romance).


SCENE & PLOT CONTEXT (the "Active scene entities" line is RANKED BY SALIENCE — when referencing a named character/threat/location, prefer the highest-salience entity matching the moment; ignore low-salience entities unless this card's strategy specifically calls for them):

I found I still could not speak.

STORY PARAMETERS:
- Tone: Earnest
- World: Fantasy
- Protagonist: Female
- Love Interest behavioral profile: The Spellbinder commands attention through presence alone. Charm is currency, and {LI_SUBJ} spends it selectively — never by accident. Three moves ahead, {LI_SUBJ} makes surrender feel like your idea.
- Love Interest: Male (use he/him pronouns IF the LI is on stage — see SCENE PRESENCE block above)
- Characters present in current scene: protagonist, love interest

PRONOUN RULE: Use correct pronouns for characters who are CURRENTLY ON STAGE. Do not use LI pronouns when the LI is not in the scene. Never use archetype labels (Storybeau, Storybelle, Storyboo) or archetype titles in any output.

TASK: Generate TWO short, contextual previews that fit THIS EXACT SCENE, obeying the CARD STRATEGY above:
1. "Do" — A specific physical action the protagonist could take RIGHT NOW (max 12 words)
2. "Say" — A specific line of dialogue the protagonist could speak RIGHT NOW (max 15 words, in quotes)

OPPOSITION RULE (CRITICAL): Temptation and Boundary are diametrically opposed choices in the player's hand. If this card is TEMPTATION, the action MUST differ in direction from what a BOUNDARY card would produce in the same scene (and vice versa). Two cards returning the same "step closer" suggestion invalidates the choice — the player cannot tell the cards apart.

These must:
- Reference actual details from the scene (location, objects, other characters)
- Match the Earnest tone
- Feel like natural continuations of what's happening
- Be more specific than the generic card suggestions
- Honor the CARD STRATEGY direction absolutely — ignore any scene momentum that would pull you toward the opposite card

Respond in this EXACT format (no labels, just two lines):
[action on first line]
[dialogue in quotes on second line]
